title: Leveraging LLM-Based Agentic Systems to Generate Quantum Applications for Test Optimization
authors: Ming Tao, Yuechen Li, Tao Yue, Man Zhang, Aitor Arrieta Marcos
abstract: Quantum computing is increasingly explored for software engineering (SE) optimization, but translating natural-language (NL) task-level requirements into executable quantum applications still demands substantial quantum and programming expertise. We present QPipe, a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent architecture that autonomously turns NL requirements into traceable quantum-application workflows through specialized agents for requirement parsing, formulation, code generation, review, execution, and verification. We evaluate QPipe on 20 NL requirements, each associated with a real-world benchmark and a test-optimization problem. QPipe successfully completes the key stages of quantum-application generation across requirements, achieving average rates of 100% for code compilation and 96.7% for application execution and final-result combination, with average generation costs of 260.1 seconds and 1.89M tokens per requirement. Among the generated quantum applications that execute successfully, the returned solutions outperform the offline genetic algorithm baseline in most cases. Ablation results further show that QPipe's advantage depends on retaining code-generation skills, task knowledge, review feedback, and multi-agent decomposition. These results indicate that agentic coordination can support generation of executable quantum applications for tackling test optimization problems from real-world benchmarks.
summary: This paper introduces QPipe, an LLM-based multi-agent system designed to automatically generate executable quantum applications from natural language requirements for test optimization. By coordinating specialized agents through a structured workflow, it successfully translates abstract goals into concrete quantum circuits that solve real-world benchmarks. This demonstrates the potential of agentic AI to bridge the significant expertise gap in applying quantum computing to practical software engineering problems.
main_problem: The core problem is autonomously translating high-level, natural-language (NL) requirements for Software Engineering (SE) optimization into executable quantum applications.
main_result: The proposed agentic system, QPipe, successfully generates these complex quantum applications with high success rates and generated solutions that often outperform classical baselines on test optimization benchmarks.
method: It employs a multi-agent LLM architecture (QPipe) that decomposes the task into specialized stages: parsing, encoding (mapping to QUBO/Ising), code generation, review, and verification.
model_or_system: The system operates on quantum computing principles, formulating optimization problems as QUBO or Ising models ($\min x^	op Qx$) suitable for execution via algorithms like QAOA on simulated quantum hardware.
key_observables: Success rates (e.g., 100% compilation pass rate), solution quality measured by the Quantum Resource Ratio (QRR) compared to classical solvers, and generation costs (time/tokens).
important_parameters: Qubit budget constraints are critical, forcing the Encoding Agent to decompose large problems into smaller, manageable subproblems.
main_assumptions: The system assumes that stable formulation patterns (QUBO/QAOA) exist for TCO tasks and that agentic coordination can reliably bridge the gap between abstract language and executable quantum code.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall QPipe workflow, show ablation results proving the necessity of specific agents (like review), and compare solution quality metrics (QRR) against baselines.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the multi-agent architecture (QPipe), describes the structured workflow involving specialized agents for each step (Parse $ightarrow$ Encode $ightarrow$ CodeGen $\leftrightarrow$ Review $ightarrow$ Verify), and concludes with empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on SE tooling, the underlying challenge of translating high-level physical or computational goals into precise quantum circuit implementations is relevant to designing control protocols for complex quantum simulations or hybrid quantum-classical algorithms.
